summary: The note covers the "Mind in Motion" seminar held September 15, 2023 by the Local Health and Wellness community center, where fitness expert James Carlton and psychologist Dr. Emily Saunders explained how exercise supports mental health. It covers the physiological and psychological benefits, group sports as a source of belonging (especially for men), barriers to participation, practical strategies, community programs, and youth mentorship. It closes with a call to apply these insights in daily life and communities.
one_line: Report on the September 15, 2023 "Mind in Motion" seminar on how exercise, group sports and community programs support mental wellness.
key_facts: The "Mind in Motion" seminar was held on September 15, 2023 and organized by the Local Health and Wellness community center.
The seminar aimed to demystify mental health discussions, particularly among men, through group sports activities.
James Carlton, a fitness expert, said exercise releases endorphins, "the body's natural mood lifters," with benefits extending beyond a quick mood boost.
Dr. Emily Saunders, a psychologist, said physical exercise has become an integral part of therapy for depression, anxiety, and stress management.
Carlton cited a study from October 2023 finding that men who played team sports reported a strong sense of camaraderie and support.

Dr. Saunders said regular activity promotes neural growth, reduced inflammation, and new brain activity patterns that promote calm; the hippocampus has been shown to grow with regular aerobic exercise.
Carlton said strength training is often overlooked in mental health discussions and can have neuroprotective benefits and improve self-esteem and confidence.
Mike Anderson, a high school football coach, said cultural barriers equate emotional struggles with weakness among men and urged people to "change the narrative."
Sarah Bennett, a community swimming instructor, has seen more initially reluctant men embrace the supportive community in her swim classes.
Carlton recommended starting small, such as daily walks or joining a recreational sports league.

Dr. Saunders named psychological barriers to exercise: lack of time, fears of inadequacy, and uncertainty about benefits; she offered cognitive-behavioral strategies and advised setting realistic, measurable goals.
John Harris, director of "Fitness for All," described affordable, community-based exercise programs for people of all income levels.
Janet Lee represented "Movers and Shakers," a group encouraging physical activity among the elderly, and said tai chi and walking groups improved seniors' mental and social health.
High school athlete Kevin Thomas said a mentor who helped with sports and school stress made a huge difference.
